summary: Intown Atlanta gets back to building this week. The BeltLine approved its biggest budget ever, $265.8 million, to sprint toward a 2030 finish, while a flood-prone Peoplestown block turns into a 5-acre park sitting on a 20-million-gallon stormwater vault. Little Five Points is getting more tacos, Spelman and BronzeLens are screening films on campus all summer, and Out on Film named a new leader. And after years on the financial brink, the Atlanta Dogwood Festival confirmed it will be back in Piedmont Park in spring 2027.

topStory.headline: The BeltLine Approved Its Biggest Budget Ever: $265.8 Million to Reach the Finish Line
topStory.summary: Atlanta BeltLine, Inc. approved a record $265.8 million budget for the year ahead as it races to finish the loop by 2030, with the hardest stretch of trail still to build.
topStory.body: The Atlanta BeltLine just approved the largest budget in its history, and the number tells you how close the finish line finally is. The FY27 plan lands at $265.8 million, up from $242 million last year, as the project pushes toward its 2030 completion goal, according to SaportaReport. Atlanta BeltLine, Inc. CEO Clyde Higgs called it a tremendous year for the corridor, which now draws about 2.5 million visitors a year. More than 60 percent of them are locals, he said, the neighbors who walk, run, and bike the trail through Old Fourth Ward and out toward the southside. The money funds the emerald necklace's final and most complicated stretch, plus the affordable housing, small business, and public art programs that have grown up alongside the trail. The budget has climbed steadily since 2023, a sign of both rising construction costs and the sprint to close the loop. For neighborhoods like Peoplestown still waiting on the Southside Trail, this budget is a real marker that the hardest miles are finally getting built.
topStory.imageAlt: Walkers and cyclists on the Atlanta BeltLine Eastside Trail in spring

stories.headline: A Flood-Prone Peoplestown Block Is Becoming a 5-Acre Park (With a 20-Million-Gallon Vault Underneath)
stories.summary: Construction is well underway on a 5-acre Peoplestown greenspace built atop a massive stormwater vault meant to end decades of flooding, just north of the newest BeltLine section.
stories.body: One of Atlanta's most flood-prone blocks is turning into something the southside has wanted for years: a real park. Just north of the newest BeltLine section in Peoplestown, a 5-acre greenspace is taking shape on what used to be a residential block, according to Urbanize Atlanta. Officially it carries a mouthful of a name, the Custer Avenue Capacity Relief Multi-Benefit Stormwater Vault project, run by the City of Atlanta Department of Watershed Management. Underneath the future lawn sits the real engineering: a vault up to 30 feet deep, built to capture 20 million gallons of stormwater in an area that has flooded for decades. Construction started in earnest about a year ago. When it wraps, the site promises a new destination for Peoplestown and its historic southside neighbors, with the flood control tucked out of sight below. It is the kind of project that does two jobs at once, fixing an old drainage problem while handing the neighborhood green space it has long been owed.
stories.imageAlt: Aerial view of the Custer Avenue stormwater park under construction in Peoplestown

stories.headline: Kelly's Market, a Decatur Corner Staple, Hits the Market for $300K
stories.summary: A neighborhood market and deli near downtown Decatur has been listed for sale for $300,000, putting a longtime corner spot in play for its next owner.
stories.body: A familiar corner stop near downtown Decatur is looking for a new owner. Kelly's Market, the neighborhood market and deli, has been listed for sale for $300,000, according to Decaturish. Small corner markets like this one are the kind of low-key institution that neighbors take for granted right up until a for-sale sign goes up. Whoever steps in will inherit a spot with a built-in regular crowd just off the square. No word yet on whether a buyer plans to keep it running as a market or try something new in the space. For now, it is one to watch for anyone who has ever grabbed a sandwich there.
stories.imageAlt: Exterior of Kelly's Market near downtown Decatur

stories.headline: Taqueria Taquito Express Is Bringing Tacos and Pupusas to Little Five Points
stories.summary: The local Mexican chain filed permits for a new location on McLendon Avenue in Little Five Points, its latest spot inside the perimeter.
stories.body: More tacos are headed to Little Five Points. Local brand Taqueria Taquito Express is planning a new location at 1165 McLendon Ave. NE, based on a recent permit filing, according to What Now Atlanta. The permit covers renovations to a small, roughly 350-square-foot building to prep the new spot. Owner Chris Murphy confirmed the location to What Now Atlanta but said an opening date is still up in the air. The menu runs the full Mexican counter lineup: tacos, burritos, tortas, quesadillas, nachos, and pupusas. The chain already has about a dozen locations around metro Atlanta, and this one plants a flag right in the middle of one of the city's most walkable, character-heavy corners.
stories.imageAlt: Tacos from Taqueria Taquito Express, planning a Little Five Points location

stories.headline: The 'A Different World' Cast Reunited in Atlanta Ahead of the Netflix Reboot
stories.summary: Ahead of the September 24 Netflix reboot, the beloved HBCU sitcom's cast gathered for a panel in Atlanta during UNCF's UNITE Summit on higher education.
stories.body: Hillman College is coming back, and the road runs through Atlanta. Ahead of the September 24 debut of Netflix's reboot of A Different World, the show's cast gathered for a panel downtown during UNCF's UNITE Summit on Higher Education, according to Capital B Atlanta. The original ran from 1987 to 1993 as a Cosby Show spinoff set at the fictional HBCU, and it is often credited with boosting real HBCU enrollment by roughly a quarter during its run. The 10-episode reboot brings back beloved characters while introducing a new generation of students. The new series takes on contemporary campus issues, from funding challenges to immigration and learning accommodations. The panel featured creator and showrunner Felicia Pride alongside returning cast, a fitting stop in a city full of the HBCUs that inspired the show in the first place.
stories.imageAlt: The A Different World cast on a panel in Atlanta ahead of the Netflix reboot

stories.headline: Spelman and BronzeLens Team Up for Weekly Film Screenings on Campus
stories.summary: Spelman's arts center is hosting a weekly BronzeLens Encore screening series through August 6, the latest chapter in a growing partnership between the college and the film festival.
stories.body: A partnership years in the making is filling Spelman's campus with film this summer. The Mary Schmidt Campbell Center for Innovation and the Arts hosted the second installment of the BLFF Encore Series on Thursday, part of a new collaboration between Spelman College and the BronzeLens Film Festival, according to The Atlanta Voice. The series runs weekly on Thursdays through Aug. 6, with each night built around a distinct theme. Thursday's program centered on family, following a July 16 opening night themed around Afrofuturism. BronzeLens director and founder Kathleen Bertrand, a Spelman graduate herself, said the partnership grew out of years of the festival holding events on the campus. For film lovers on the west side, it is a standing Thursday reason to head to the AUC.
stories.imageAlt: A BronzeLens Encore film screening at Spelman College

stories.headline: Out on Film Names Cindy L. Abel as Its New Executive Director
stories.summary: Atlanta's LGBTQ+ film festival tapped longtime nonprofit and entertainment leader Cindy L. Abel to lead it, filling the top job after a months-long search.
stories.body: Atlanta's LGBTQ+ film festival has its new leader. Out on Film named former nonprofit executive Cindy L. Abel as its executive director, according to Rough Draft Atlanta. Abel brings more than 25 years across the nonprofit, corporate, and entertainment worlds. She previously co-chaired the Gay & Lesbian Victory Fund, served as the first executive director of Georgia Equality, and held leadership roles with the Atlanta Film Festival and Women in Film & Television Atlanta. The festival, which screens around Midtown, launched the search in April after founding executive director Justice Obiaya stepped down in March. Abel said she felt like the right person to help shepherd the festival into its next chapter.
stories.imageAlt: Cindy L. Abel, the new executive director of Out on Film

stories.headline: The Atlanta Dogwood Festival Is Coming Back to Piedmont Park in 2027
stories.summary: After years on the financial brink, the 90-plus-year-old arts festival will return to Piedmont Park April 9-11, 2027, and it is staying free.
stories.body: One of Atlanta's oldest traditions dodged the ax. The Atlanta Dogwood Festival will return to Piedmont Park from April 9 to April 11, 2027, and it will stay free, according to Fox 5 Atlanta. The festival had operated in the red for several years, hit by a roughly 30 percent jump in production costs and a drop in sponsorships that opened up a $250,000 shortfall and put the 2026 edition in real danger. Stronger donations, corporate sponsors, and foundation backing helped close the gap, and organizers say the event finally turned a profit. Organizers have not released the full artist lineup or entertainment schedule yet. But for one of the country's longest-running arts festivals, simply confirming next spring's dates is the headline.
stories.imageAlt: Crowds at the Atlanta Dogwood Festival in Piedmont Park
